title: Do people prefer traditional architecture? - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: A survey of roughly twenty properly sampled visual preference surveys since the 1990s finds that traditional architecture is preferred by 60 to 90 percent of respondents in every study, across Britain, the US, the Netherlands, Portugal, Canada and Chile, with almost no variation by age, gender, politics, class or income. Architects are the striking exception, preferring the opposite, and AI-generated image pairs have recently made these surveys cheap and tightly controlled — leaving a puzzle of why more than 99 percent of architects still practice styles the public says it dislikes.

themes.theme: The headline result: traditional wins everywhere

insights.claim: Across roughly twenty properly sampled visual preference surveys run since the 1990s, over 60 percent of respondents have favored traditional architecture in every single survey, with many showing over 85 percent support.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A consistent 60-90 percent latent demand for traditional design is an unexploited product gap in housing and commercial development, since almost no supply is built to it.
insights.quote: In every survey conducted, over 60 percent of the respondents have favored traditional architecture, with many revealing over 85 percent support.
insights.locator: Were Summerson and von Eckhardt right?

insights.claim: The author's provisional conclusion is that 70 to 90 percent of the population has a clear preference for traditional architecture, and that every demographic group favors it — men and women, old and young, rich and poor.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Design preference is close to demographically invariant, so developers cannot segment their way out of it; the same facade strategy plays across all customer cohorts.
insights.quote: Every demographic group favors traditional design: men and women, old and young, rich and poor.
insights.locator: For now, the provisional conclusion

insights.claim: The preference for traditional styles holds not only for houses but also for hospitals and commercial and civic buildings.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The finding generalizes beyond residential, so the commercial case for traditional facades extends to healthcare, office and public-sector procurement.
insights.quote: This holds not only for houses but also for hospitals and commercial and civic buildings.
insights.locator: However, to the extent that their findings are reliable

insights.claim: In David Halpern's 1987 Cambridge study, students across disciplines agreed on which of twelve faces were attractive, but architecture students' building preferences were wildly different from, and often directly opposite to, those of other students.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The divergence is specific to trained architects, not to aesthetics in general — evidence that professional gatekeepers systematically mis-forecast end-user demand.
insights.quote: But when it came to buildings, architecture students held wildly different views from those in other disciplines. In fact, their preferences were often directly opposite.
insights.locator: Britain’s cottage industry in architectural visual preference surveying

insights.claim: Halpern's expert-versus-lay divergence has been replicated in Canada in 2001, Britain in 2015 and Chile in 2019, and again in Luis Balula's 2008-2009 Évora study where non-experts rated pastiche Mediterranean homes positively and a modernist apartment block negatively while experts did the reverse.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The gap is stable across four decades and five countries, which makes it a structural feature of the industry rather than a local quirk.
insights.locator: David Halpern’s finding that architecture students differ

insights.claim: British public body CABE, which commissioned surveys in 2002 and 2005, found low support for modern styles and expressed surprise, writing that modernism's concern for light and large windows 'should give a modern style a clear advantage' over traditional designs.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Even survey sponsors hostile to the traditionalist thesis reproduced the result, which materially weakens the 'loaded images' objection.
insights.quote: ‘The Modern Movement’s concern for light and sun and large windows should give a modern style a clear advantage over more traditional designs, but this advantage does not seem to have been understood by home buyers’
insights.locator: Perhaps the difference between lay and expert taste

insights.claim: The National Civic Art Society's 2020 survey of US federal and courthouse buildings, controlling for massing and context across seven photo pairs, found traditional designs preferred by an average of 72 percent.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Public-building procurement is where this preference can be converted into policy fastest, since the client is the state and the evidence base is now specific to federal architecture.
insights.locator: Perhaps the most famous visual preference survey

insights.claim: The US federal-building result was almost uncorrelated with politics: 70 percent of Democrats and 73 percent of Republicans preferred traditional designs, with women at 77 versus men at 67, and only weak age effects (77 percent of over-65s versus 68 percent of 18-34s).
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Architecture is one of the rare policy questions with no partisan split, which makes traditionalist design mandates unusually cheap politically to enact.
insights.quote: There was almost no correlation with political affiliation, with 70 percent of Democrats and 73 percent of Republicans preferring the traditional designs.
insights.locator: As in other studies, most striking is how little

insights.claim: A 2023 Create Streets poll on rival designs for a Bath rugby stadium found 74 to 26 percent support for Apollodorus Architecture's classical scheme over the utilitarian proposal, with even 18-24 year olds preferring the traditional design 61 to 39.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Young cohorts, usually assumed to be the modernist constituency, still break traditional by a 20-point margin — there is no generational bailout coming for modernist design.
insights.locator: In 2023, disappointed by the utilitarian design proposal

insights.claim: For HS2, the railway under construction between London and Birmingham, respondents preferred a red-brick-clad viaduct emulating nineteenth-century designs over the planned concrete viaducts by 69 to 28 percent, with Labour voters marginally more pro-traditional than Conservatives (72 versus 69) and younger respondents more traditional than older ones.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Infrastructure cladding is a low-cost lever on public consent for megaprojects; facade treatment may buy political goodwill more cheaply than route or capacity concessions.
insights.locator: The same trend shows up in infrastructure.

insights.claim: When Christ's College Cambridge proposed a library by Grafton Architects, one of the world's most prestigious firms, a survey of over 2,000 British adults preferred a Gothic counterproposal 71 percent to 21 percent.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Prestige-firm branding does not protect a modernist scheme in public opinion, which erodes the reputational premium star architects command from institutional clients.
insights.locator: In 2025, Christ’s College Cambridge announced plans

insights.claim: On Marks and Spencer's plan to demolish a 1920s Oxford Street building, a poll of 3,130 British adults preferred a Francis Terry facade-retention scheme with the same floor area by 79 to 17 percent — the strongest margin in any Create Streets study — and even Londoners favored it 72 to 26.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Retrofit-and-extend schemes can match floor area while polling far better than demolition, which is a reputational and planning-risk argument retail landlords can monetize.
insights.locator: The British retailer Marks and Spencer

insights.claim: The Aesthetic City's 2025 Dutch survey found traditional preference ranging from 67 to 92 percent across eight image pairs, averaging 82 percent, confirming the pattern holds in continental Europe.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The result is not an Anglo-American artifact; European planning politics is the next place this evidence base gets deployed.
insights.locator: Continental Europeans appear to prefer traditional architecture

insights.claim: Artificial intelligence has sharply cut the time and cost of producing comparable survey images, making large-scale, tightly controlled visual preference surveys feasible for the first time and triggering what the piece calls a golden age of the method.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Cheap AI image generation turns aesthetic preference into a measurable, poll-able variable — expect it to be used as a weapon in planning disputes and as a pre-build market-research tool by developers.
insights.quote: In the past few years, artificial intelligence has greatly reduced the time and costs of producing comparable images, making reliable large-scale visual preference surveys far more feasible.
insights.locator: Early visual preference surveys were often methodologically primitive

insights.claim: In the Dutch study, all but one image pair was built by photographing a real modernist building and using AI to generate the traditional alternative, allowing tight control for context, weather and massing.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: This is a concrete, replicable methodology: any developer or campaign group can now A/B test a facade against an AI-generated counterfactual before committing capital.
insights.quote: they used a photograph of a modernist building and then used AI to create the traditional alternative
insights.locator: The Dutch study is notable

insights.claim: Most visual preference surveys have been commissioned by organizations sympathetic to traditional architecture, and skeptics argue results only show that the particular modernist example chosen was weak.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The selection-bias objection is the main thing that would need to break for the traditionalist case to be discounted; a neutral or hostile sponsor replicating the result would be the decisive data point.
insights.quote: The suspicion of a loaded choice of images is heightened by the fact that most visual preference surveys have been commissioned by organizations sympathetic to traditional architecture
insights.locator: Taking the measure of public taste

insights.claim: The field is still tiny: perhaps only three dozen fully controlled image pairs have ever been polled, and only in Britain, the Netherlands and the United States, with the evidence base expected to triple or quadruple within a decade.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Conviction should be sized to a thin dataset — but the direction of travel is one-way so far, since every controlled pair surveyed has pointed the same way.
insights.quote: perhaps only three dozen fully controlled image pairs have ever been polled on
insights.locator: Nevertheless, it is striking

insights.claim: The Shoreditch Works survey deliberately stacked the deck against traditionalism by comparing existing low-rise postwar warehouses with much taller proposed blocks in a Victorian and Art Deco idiom, yet 76 to 78 percent still preferred the proposed scheme.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Traditional styling appears to buy public tolerance for greater height and density — a potentially large unlock for developers fighting objections to tall buildings.
insights.quote: The standard view is that the public dislikes high-rise development, meaning that this study could be seen as ‘biased against’ traditional architecture.
insights.locator: Create Streets recently ran a slightly different kind of poll

insights.claim: Almost every architecture school in the world teaches only broadly modernist styles and probably more than 99 percent of architects practice exclusively in them, producing a mysterious divergence between what the public says it wants and what actually gets commissioned.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Supply is constrained by professional training and norms, not by demand or regulation — so the bottleneck to arbitraging this gap is finding practitioners, which is where a scarce-skill premium sits.
insights.quote: Almost every architectural school in the world exclusively teaches broadly modernist styles, and probably more than 99 percent of architects practice exclusively in them.
insights.locator: If this is true, a greater puzzle comes into view

insights.claim: In Britain there has been hardly a single public commission in a traditional style since the 1950s, and traditional styles have been virtually extinct for seven decades except in the market for private housing.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Private housing is the one segment where revealed and stated preference already align, which is a tell that in competitive consumer markets traditional design does get built and does sell.
insights.quote: Except in the market for private housing, traditional styles have been virtually extinct for seven decades.
insights.locator: In Britain, there has been hardly a single public commission

insights.claim: The persistence of modernist commissioning cannot be fully blamed on anti-traditional planning rules, because the same trend is evident in jurisdictions whose development control systems are stylistically neutral.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Deregulating style codes alone would not shift what gets built; the constraint is inside the profession, which changes what a policy intervention would have to target.
insights.quote: the broad trend is still evident in jurisdictions whose development control systems are stylistically neutral
insights.locator: Although in some cases this can be explained

insights.claim: A 1998 British Market Research Bureau survey for the Popular Housing Forum found 94 percent of potential newbuild buyers would prefer a more traditional option and 92 percent of other respondents wanted a traditional option built near them.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: NIMBY resistance to new housing may be partly a style objection rather than a density objection — traditional facades could measurably reduce local opposition to newbuild supply.
insights.quote: 94 percent of potential newbuild buyers said they would prefer to live in one of the more traditional options
insights.locator: The first properly sampled visual preference survey followed in 1998

insights.claim: In a 2009 ADAM Architecture survey using matched perspectives and lighting, two prize-winning modernist commercial buildings drew only 23 percent support against 77 percent for two traditional designs.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Award-winning quality does not rescue modernist commercial designs in public preference, which undercuts the 'pick better modernism' rebuttal.
insights.quote: Both of the modernist buildings had won prizes, suggesting that they were especially well-designed examples. Even so, only 23 percent of respondents preferred them, compared to 77 percent for the two traditional designs.
insights.locator: One of the best early visual preference surveys

insights.claim: Visual preference surveying began in 1979 when Metuchen, New Jersey commissioned the Rutgers University Urban Design Studio, whose finding that residents overwhelmingly preferred detailed facades, walkable human scale and traditional streetscapes was surprising at the time and led the town to adopt a design code.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The method's original purpose was to justify municipal design codes with data — the same playbook now being run at national scale, and a template for how the evidence converts into binding rules.
insights.quote: The Metuchen survey was the first to show that people tend to have predictable, shared responses to different built environments, responses that are not purely a matter of individual taste.
insights.locator: The birth of visual preference surveying

insights.claim: Both supporters and detractors of modernism have long agreed it is unpopular, with John Summerson noting in 1940 that the public 'can't understand it, never will, and hates it like poison' and Wolf von Eckardt claiming in 1977 that 'No one mourned. It was never popular.'
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The unpopularity of modernism is not a recent traditionalist talking point; it was conceded by the movement's own sympathizers eighty years ago.
insights.quote: ‘can’t understand it, never will, and hates it like poison’
insights.locator: In the twentieth century, a radical change
